name: map()
what_it_does: Applies a function to every item of an iterable, producing a new sequence of the results, without writing an explicit loop.
parameters: function - a function (or lambda) that takes one item and returns a new value. iterable - what to apply it to.
return_value: A map object (lazy) - usually wrapped in list() to see the results, or consumed directly in a for loop.
example:
numbers = [1, 2, 3]
doubled = list(map(lambda x: x * 2, numbers))
print(doubled)
common_mistakes: Forgetting map() returns a lazy map object, not a list - printing it directly shows something like <map object at 0x...> instead of the values, until you wrap it in list(). A list comprehension ([x * 2 for x in numbers]) does the same thing and is often considered more readable in Python.
when_to_use: Transforming every item in a collection the same way - though for most simple cases, a list comprehension is the more idiomatic Python choice.
